summary: The king who shut the old gods' temples for one sun disc, and the queen whose painted face became the most copied image in Egyptian art.
look: You meet their faces at the GEM on the 11th and the Luxor Museum on the 22nd: long-chinned, full-lipped colossi from Karnak and the talatat wall of small sandstone blocks. Recognise their art by elongated heads, soft bellies and thin limbs, and by the Aten above them, a sun disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding the ankh sign of life. Their names and faces are often hacked out.
story:
Amenhotep IV was a younger son of Amenhotep III and Tiye who became heir when his brother Thutmose died. He took the throne around 1353 BC and at first ruled conventionally, though he soon built temples to the Aten at Karnak from small standard blocks now called talatat. Around his year 5 he renamed himself Akhenaten, 'effective for the Aten', and founded a new capital, Akhetaten, 'horizon of the Aten', at Amarna. Amun's cult was abandoned and his name hacked from monuments. The Great Hymn to the Aten, carved in the Amarna tomb of the courtier Ay, has often been compared with Psalm 104. Whether this was true monotheism is still argued.

Nefertiti, 'the beautiful one has come', is of unknown origin; Ay may have been her father. She and Akhenaten had six daughters. On early Karnak blocks she appears almost twice as often as the king and even smites enemies, a royal pose. Later she fades from the record. Some scholars identify her with the female king Neferneferuaten who reigned briefly after Akhenaten; others disagree. Her painted bust was found in 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt's German team in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna and is in Berlin; Egypt has asked for it back.

Akhenaten died around 1336 BC. Within a few years the court left Amarna, and later kings called him 'the enemy' or 'that criminal'. DNA studies published in 2010 identified the man buried in KV55 as Tutankhamun's father, possibly Akhenaten, though both the results and the identification are debated.
details: The Aten: a sun disc with rays ending in hands; the hands near the royal faces hold the ankh sign of life.
The Aten's names are written in two cartouches, like a king's: the god was presented as a heavenly king.
GEM colossi from Karnak: long jaw, slit eyes, swelling hips; one figure may show Nefertiti, scholars disagree.
Luxor Museum (22nd): the talatat wall, hundreds of small blocks reassembled from Akhenaten's Karnak temple.
Tutankhamun's golden throne (GEM): the Aten still shines over the young couple, a leftover of Amarna days.
fun_fact: The talatat blocks survive because later kings dumped them as rubble inside Karnak's pylons, where they waited, packed and hidden, for over 3,000 years.
narration: Few couples have changed a country so fast. Akhenaten was born Amenhotep, a younger son of Amenhotep the Third and Queen Tiye, and became king about 1353 BC. Within 5 years he had renamed himself Akhenaten, effective for the Aten, and was building a brand new capital in the desert at Amarna. The Aten was the sun disc itself, drawn with rays that end in little hands, some holding out the sign of life. Amun's temples lost their support, and his name was chiselled off walls across Egypt. Was it the first monotheism? Egyptologists still argue: perhaps it was one god for the royal family, with the king as the only way to reach him. The art changed too: long faces, heavy hips, the family kissing and playing with their daughters. Nefertiti, whose name means the beautiful one has come, was more than a consort. On early temple blocks she appears almost twice as often as her husband, even smiting enemies. She bore 6 daughters, then fades from the record. Some scholars think she ruled briefly as a female king. Her famous painted bust was dug up in 1912 by a German team in a sculptor's workshop and is now in Berlin. After Akhenaten died, his city was abandoned and his successors called him that criminal. Look at the faces: the slanting eyes and drooping chin are the Amarna style, impossible to mistake.

summary: A minor boy king, erased from the king lists, who became the most famous pharaoh only because his tomb was forgotten and survived nearly intact.
look: He is the man behind the GEM's Tutankhamun galleries on the 11th and the small tomb KV62 on the 21st, where his mummy still lies. His throne name, Nebkheperure, is a sun disc, a scarab, three plural strokes and a basket. His birth name puts the god Amun first in the cartouche, out of respect, and ends with the ankh.
story:
Born around 1342 BC as Tutankhaten, 'living image of the Aten', he was a king's son at Amarna. DNA tests published in 2010 point to the man in KV55 as his father and to the 'Younger Lady' of KV35 as his mother, a full sister of that man; the results and the identifications are still debated. His wet nurse Maia had her own tomb at Saqqara. He became king at 8 or 9 and married Ankhesenpaaten, a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti.

His advisers, probably including Ay and the general Horemheb, steered the reversal. The court left Amarna, the Aten lost his place, Amun returned, and the couple became Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. The Restoration Stela, found at Karnak in 1905, describes temples in ruin and the king renewing cult images and priesthoods. He died at about 19, around 1323 BC. A 2012 study suggested malaria combined with a leg fracture; the bone fragments in his skull, once proof of murder for some, were caused after death. Two stillborn daughters lay in his tomb.

Hittite records tell of an Egyptian queen, called Dakhamunzu, who begged King Suppiluliuma for a son to marry; the prince Zannanza died on the way. She is most often identified with Ankhesenamun. Ay succeeded, then Horemheb, who usurped Tutankhamun's monuments and left the Amarna kings off the lists. A minor reign, forgotten, under rubble: that is why KV62 still held over 5,000 objects when Howard Carter found it in 1922.
details: His cartouche: Amun (reed leaf, game board, water) first out of respect, then Tut (loaf, chick, loaf) and the ankh.
Throne name Nebkheperure: sun disc, scarab, three plural strokes and a basket. It is stamped on many of his objects.
KV62 (21st): the mummy lies in a glass case; the burial chamber shows Ay performing the Opening of the Mouth.
At the GEM, look for his walking sticks: well over 100 were buried with him, and scans suggest a deformed left foot.
The Restoration Stela, found at Karnak in 1905: his decree reopening the temples, with his names later recut by Horemheb.
fun_fact: His tomb's entrance lay under workmen's huts and rubble from the later tomb of Ramesses VI, one reason robbers missed most of it after the first break-ins.
narration: Tutankhamun was a small king with a gigantic afterlife. He was born about 1342 BC as Tutankhaten, living image of the Aten, in the heretic city of Amarna. DNA tests suggest his father was the man buried in K V 55, probably Akhenaten, and his mother a full sister of that man, though not every expert trusts the results. He became king at 8 or 9 and married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. His advisers, not the child, steered the great U-turn: the court left Amarna, the old gods came back, and the royal couple changed their names to Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. He died at about 19. For years people said he was murdered, because of bone fragments in his skull, but scans show the damage happened after death. A broken leg and malaria are the leading suspects now. Two tiny daughters, born too early to live, were buried with him. Then something strange happens. Hittite archives record that an Egyptian queen, very likely his widow, wrote to the Hittite king: my husband is dead, I have no son, send me one of yours. A prince set out and died on the road. Tutankhamun's successors erased his name, so later Egyptians forgot him, and so did the tomb robbers. That is why his tomb survived. Look at his cartouche: the god Amun is written first, out of respect, though you say it last.

summary: A father who paid for the finest reliefs in Egypt, and a son who put his own name on everything, including other kings' statues.
look: Ramesses II is the face of this trip: the GEM atrium colossus on the 11th, Abu Simbel on the 17th, the Ramesseum on the 21st, Luxor Temple's pylon and Karnak on the 22nd. Spot his throne name Usermaatre Setepenre: a sun disc and the goddess Maat holding a was sceptre. Seti I's work is subtler: delicate raised relief in the north half of Karnak's Hypostyle Hall and in his tomb, while his son's is often deep, bold sunk relief.
story:
Seti I, 'man of Seth', succeeded his father Ramesses I, an elderly vizier and soldier whom Horemheb had named heir. Reigning about 1290 to 1279 BC, Seti restored order after Amarna, campaigned in Canaan, Syria and Libya and briefly took Kadesh; his battle scenes cover the north outer wall of Karnak's Hypostyle Hall. His temple at Abydos and his tomb, KV17, found by Belzoni in 1817 and decorated in every passage, hold some of the finest relief carving in Egypt.

Ramesses II was not born a prince; he was about 11 when his grandfather was named heir. Made prince regent at about 14, he took the throne at about 25 in 1279 BC and ruled 66 years, dying around 90 in 1213 BC. He moved the capital to Pi-Ramesses in the Delta. In year 5, at Kadesh, the Hittite king Muwatalli caught his divided army off guard; Ramesses rallied, reinforcements arrived, and the battle ended in a stalemate that his temples call a triumph. In year 21 he made peace with the Hittites, in a treaty preserved in both Egyptian hieroglyphs and Hittite cuneiform, and later married Hittite princesses.

He celebrated 13 or 14 Sed festivals, fathered more than 100 children and built or usurped on a colossal scale, often recutting older kings' names. His mummy, from the 1881 royal cache, is at NMEC. The Greeks called him Ozymandias, from his throne name Usermaatre. There is no evidence either way that he was the pharaoh of the Exodus.
details: Usermaatre: a sun disc above the goddess Maat holding a was sceptre. Setepenre adds an adze sign, water and another sun.
Karnak Hypostyle (22nd): north half in Seti's delicate raised relief, south half in Ramesses' deeper sunk relief.
Kadesh reliefs: the giant king alone in his chariot firing arrows, and the fortress ringed by the river Orontes.
Usurped statues: freshly cut, extra-deep cartouches on older smooth surfaces, sometimes with a ghost of an earlier name.
Karnak's north outer wall: Seti's campaign scenes, with the forts and wells along the Sinai road each drawn and named.
fun_fact: Shelley's sonnet Ozymandias, with its 'vast and trunkless legs of stone', is usually linked to Ramesses' fallen colossus at the Ramesseum, which you see on the 21st.
narration: You will meet Ramesses the Second more than anyone else on this trip, so meet his father first. Seti the First, whose name means man of Seth, was the son of an army officer who had been handed the throne. He restored order after the Amarna years, fought in Canaan and Syria, and paid for some of the most refined carving in Egypt: his temple at Abydos and his tomb in the Valley, the longest of all. His son Ramesses came to the throne at about 25 and ruled for 66 years. He died around 90, having outlived many of his more than 100 children. In his 5th year, at Kadesh in Syria, he walked into a Hittite ambush. His army was split, he fought his way out, and reinforcements saved the day. The result was a draw, but he had it carved as a glorious victory on temple after temple. 16 years later he made peace with the Hittites, in a treaty whose text survives in both sides' versions, and later married a Hittite princess. He also loved to recarve older kings' statues with his own name. The Greeks knew him as Ozymandias, from his throne name Usermaatre. His mummy, now at NMEC, was flown to Paris in 1976 for treatment, and the story goes that he was issued a passport giving his occupation as king, deceased. Look for his cartouche: a sun disc, and the seated goddess with her feather and an animal-headed sceptre.

summary: When the Bronze Age world collapsed around 1200 BC, Ramesses III held Egypt together, then was murdered in a plot from his own harem.
look: His memorial is Medinet Habu on the West Bank, which you see on the 21st, with the Sea Peoples battles carved on its walls; his tomb is KV11. Recognise him by his throne name Usermaatre Meryamun, a near copy of Ramesses II's, and by the feathered and horned helmets of his enemies in the reliefs.
story:
Ramesses III was the son of Setnakhte, founder of the 20th Dynasty, and only distantly related to Ramesses II, whom he copied down to his throne name. He reigned about 31 years, from around 1186 BC. He repelled Libyan invasions in years 5 and 11, and in year 8 the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, Denyen, Sherden and Tjeker, who came by land and sea. He beat them in Djahy and in the Nile mouths, where archers lined the banks. The Peleset settled in Canaan and are usually identified with the Philistines.

Around him the Late Bronze Age world was breaking up: the Hittite empire, Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces fell between the late 13th and early 12th centuries BC. Drought, earthquakes, migration and failing trade are all blamed; recent work suggests fewer cities burned than once thought.

Egypt survived, poorer. In year 29 the unpaid tomb builders of Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded strike. Then a minor wife, Tiye, plotted to put her son Pentawere on the throne. Trial papyri record 38 death sentences, and a CT scan published in 2012 showed the king's throat cut to the bone. His chosen heir, Ramesses IV, succeeded anyway.
details: Medinet Habu (21st): the sea battle on the outer north wall is often called the oldest picture of a naval battle.
Headgear: Peleset and Denyen wear feathered crowns, Sherden horned helmets; Sherden also served Egypt as guards.
Look for scribes counting the severed hands of dead enemies: the army's grim way of keeping a tally.
KV11 (21st): a side chamber painted with two harpists gave it the name Harpers' Tomb.
fun_fact: During the trial, some of the accused harem women tried to seduce their judges; they were caught, and the judges were punished too.
narration: Ramesses the Third is often called the last great pharaoh. He ruled for about 31 years, from around 1186 BC, and modelled himself on Ramesses the Second, even copying his throne name. His world was falling apart. Around 1200 BC the Hittite empire, the trading city of Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces of Greece all went down. Drought, earthquakes, migrations and broken trade all played a part. In his 8th year a coalition Egypt called the Sea Peoples attacked by land and sea. He beat them in the Nile mouths, with archers lining the banks and grappling hooks to drag the ships in. One group, the Peleset, probably became the Philistines. But the cost was high. In year 29 the royal tomb builders went unpaid and staged the first recorded strike in history. Then a minor queen, Tiye, plotted to put her son on the throne. The trial records survive, and CT scans show the king's throat was cut to the bone. Look at the reliefs for the Sea Peoples' feathered headdresses and horned helmets.

summary: Kings from Napata in today's Sudan conquered Egypt in the name of Amun, ruled it for nearly a century and fought the Assyrians to the end.
look: You meet them in Aswan's Nubian Museum on the 18th or 19th, and at Karnak on the 22nd, where one tall papyrus column in the Great Court is all that stands of Taharqa's kiosk. Recognise a Kushite king by the close-fitting cap crown with two cobras on the brow instead of one, and by faces carved in a deliberately old-fashioned style.
story:
Kush, the kingdom around Napata in today's Sudan, had absorbed Egyptian religion during centuries of New Kingdom rule, and its kings worshipped Amun at Gebel Barkal. Piye, who ruled from about 744 to 714 BC, already controlled Upper Egypt when Tefnakht of Sais led a coalition of Delta rulers south. In his 20th year Piye marched north, celebrated Opet at Thebes, took Hermopolis after a five-month siege, stormed Memphis and received the submission of the Delta kings. His victory stela at Gebel Barkal presents the campaign as a holy war. Then he went home to Napata.

His successors, Shabaka and Shebitku, whose order is debated, ruled Egypt directly. Taharqa, king from 690 to 664 BC, enjoyed a huge Nile flood in his 6th year and built at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal. The Bible calls him Tirhakah, sent against the Assyrian Sennacherib in 701 BC. Taharqa beat the Assyrian Esarhaddon in 674 BC, but in 671 Esarhaddon took Memphis and captured the royal family. Ashurbanipal pressed on, and after Taharqa's death his successor Tantamani's counter-attack ended with the Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC. Taharqa lies under the largest pyramid at Nuri. Kushite art deliberately revived Old and Middle Kingdom styles.
details: Double uraeus: two cobras side by side on the brow, probably for the two kingdoms of Kush and Egypt.
Karnak Great Court (22nd): the lone papyrus column standing in the court is all that remains of Taharqa's kiosk.
Kushite royal portraits: round heads, broad cheeks, a close cap crown and often ram-head amulets at the neck.
Archaism: Kushite sculptors copied Old Kingdom models, so a statue can look 2,000 years older than it is.
Aswan's Nubian Museum (18th or 19th) tells their story from the Kushite side; look for the double cobras.
fun_fact: Remains of three colossal statues of Taharqa were found at the gate of the Assyrian palace at Nineveh, most likely carried off as war trophies.
narration: For nearly a century, Egypt was ruled from what is now Sudan. The kings of Kush, at Napata near the holy mountain of Gebel Barkal, worshipped Amun as devoutly as any Theban. When the princes of the Delta squabbled, King Piye marched north, in the 720s BC. He stopped at Thebes for the Opet festival, ordered his soldiers to purify themselves before battle, and took city after city. His victory stela says that at Hermopolis what angered him most was finding the horses starved. Then he sailed home and never came back. His successors stayed. Taharqa, from 690 BC, built at Karnak and across Nubia, and the Bible remembers him as Tirhakah, marching against the Assyrians. In the end the Assyrians won, took Memphis, and in 663 BC sacked Thebes itself. Taharqa was buried under the biggest pyramid at Nuri, with more than 1,000 shabtis. Look for a Kushite king's crown: a tight cap with 2 cobras on the forehead.

summary: For 300 years Greek-speaking kings from Macedon ruled Egypt as pharaohs, and the last of them, Cleopatra, was the first to learn Egyptian.
look: Their temples fill your 20th (Kom Ombo, Edfu, Esna) and Philae in Aswan; Alexander himself waits at Siwa on the 13th-15th and in Luxor Temple's barque shrine on the 22nd. Recognise a Ptolemy by a cartouche spelled out sign by sign, often followed by 'living forever, beloved of Ptah'. Ptolemaic reliefs are crowded and deeply cut, with fleshy, rounded figures quite unlike New Kingdom work.
story:
Alexander reached Egypt late in 332 BC, and the Persian satrap surrendered. He honoured the Apis bull at Memphis, founded Alexandria on the coast and crossed the desert to Siwa, where the oracle of Amun, Zeus-Ammon to the Greeks, hailed him as the god's son. He died in Babylon in 323 BC. His bodyguard Ptolemy, son of Lagos, took Egypt as satrap, intercepted Alexander's body on its way to Macedon and buried it at Memphis, later in Alexandria; the tomb has never been found. Ptolemy called himself king from 305 BC and launched the Library and the Lighthouse.

His descendants ruled until 30 BC. They spoke Greek, lived in Alexandria and, from Ptolemy II and Arsinoe II on, often married their siblings. Crowned by the priests of Ptah at Memphis, they paid for traditional temples to keep the priesthood loyal: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae, Esna and Dendera all carry Ptolemaic cartouches. The Rosetta Stone is a priestly decree of 196 BC honouring Ptolemy V.

Cleopatra VII, born in 69 BC, was the first of her family known to learn Egyptian. Fighting her brother Ptolemy XIII, she allied with Julius Caesar, who arrived in 48 BC, and bore him Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she joined Mark Antony, whom she met at Tarsos in 41 BC; they had three children, and the Donations of Alexandria gave them kingdoms. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC and took Alexandria in 30. Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra died in August, most likely by poison. Egypt passed to Rome, under Octavian's personal control.
details: In a Ptolemy cartouche, the easy signs are a stool for p, a loaf for t, a lion for l and a folded cloth for s.
Edfu (20th): the king offering to Horus is usually a Ptolemy; the temple was built between 237 and 57 BC.
Luxor Temple (22nd): the barque shrine shows Alexander as pharaoh in Egyptian crowns, offering to Amun.
Siwa (13th-15th): the oracle temple at Aghurmi, where Alexander consulted Amun in 331 BC.
Look for Greek letters among the graffiti at Philae and Edfu: your alphabet on Egyptian walls.
fun_fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
narration: For a Greek visitor, this is your chapter of Egyptian history. In late 332 BC Alexander the Great marched into Egypt and the Persian governor gave up without a fight. Alexander honoured the Apis bull at Memphis, founded Alexandria on the coast, and crossed the desert to Siwa, where the oracle of Amun greeted him as the son of the god. 9 years later he was dead in Babylon. His general Ptolemy, son of Lagos, took Egypt, and even hijacked Alexander's body on its way home to Macedon and buried it in Egypt. That tomb has never been found. Ptolemy's family ruled for almost 300 years. They spoke Greek, lived in Alexandria, collected books for the great Library, and often married their own sisters. To keep the Egyptian priests happy, they built temples in the old style: Edfu, Kom Ombo, Philae, Esna. On their walls a Macedonian king in a pharaoh's kilt offers to Horus. The last of the line, Cleopatra the Seventh, was the first of her family known to speak Egyptian. She allied herself first with Julius Caesar, with whom she had a son, then with Mark Antony. After their defeat at Actium in 31 BC, Antony killed himself, and Cleopatra died soon after, probably by poison rather than the bite of an asp. Egypt became Rome's. Look at any Ptolemy's cartouche: you can spell out the Greek name, sign by sign.

period: New Kingdom to Late Period, c. 1550-525 BC
summary: Egypt's queens could be priests, diplomats and even kings, and for two centuries unmarried princesses held power in Thebes as God's Wives of Amun.
look: Queens appear smaller than the king but in their own crowns: the vulture cap, two tall plumes, or cow horns and sun disc. You meet Nefertari at Abu Simbel's small temple on the 17th and in her tomb on the 21st, and Tiye beside her husband in the museums. A God's Wife of Amun wears a close cap with plumes, and her name sits in a cartouche like a king's.
story:
A Great Royal Wife had her own household, titles and ritual roles. Ahmose-Nefertari, wife of Ahmose I, was the first queen to hold the office of God's Wife of Amun at Karnak; after her death she was worshipped at Deir el-Medina, often painted with black skin, the colour of fertile earth and rebirth. Hatshepsut held the same office before becoming king. Tiye, daughter of the courtiers Yuya and Thuya, was written to directly by foreign rulers. Nefertari exchanged letters with the Hittite queen Puduhepa. Tausert ruled as king at the end of the 19th Dynasty.

From Ramesses VI on, the God's Wife was an unmarried king's daughter who adopted her successor. In the 25th and 26th Dynasties these women were the face of royal power in Thebes. Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III, adopted Amenirdis I, daughter of the Kushite king Kashta; in 656 BC Psamtik I made Piye's daughter Shepenupet II adopt his own daughter Nitocris. The office ended when the Persians conquered Egypt in 525 BC.

Ordinary Egyptian women could own and inherit property, make contracts, divorce and go to court. Herodotus was amazed that in Egypt women went to market while men stayed home at the loom.
details: Abu Simbel small temple (17th): Nefertari's standing statues on the facade are as tall as Ramesses' own.
Queens' crowns: the vulture cap with wings over the ears, two tall plumes, and often Hathor's horns and sun disc.
Medinet Habu (21st): the funerary chapels of the God's Wives Amenirdis and Shepenupet stand inside the enclosure, near the gate.
Deir el-Medina (21st): Ahmose-Nefertari, patron of the village, often appears with black skin in tomb paintings.
Nefertari's tomb, QV66 (21st): the queen plays senet and offers to the gods alone, a tomb as fine as any king's.
fun_fact: When Psamtik I reunited Egypt in 656 BC, he took over Thebes partly by adoption papers: the reigning God's Wife had to adopt his daughter Nitocris as her heir.
narration: Egyptian queens were far more than wives. Ahmose-Nefertari, wife of the king who drove out the Hyksos, became the first God's Wife of Amun, a powerful priestly office at Karnak. Later she was worshipped as a goddess by the tomb builders, and painted with black skin, the colour of fertile earth. Queen Tiye, a courtier's daughter, received letters from foreign kings in her own right. Nefertari wrote to the Hittite queen, and Ramesses carved her statues as tall as his own at Abu Simbel. Some women went further: Hatshepsut and later Tausert ruled as kings. Then the God's Wife became something unique. From Dynasty 20 she was a king's daughter who never married, and who adopted the next king's daughter as her heir. For about 200 years these women were the face of royal power in Thebes. Even ordinary women could own land, divorce and go to court, which amazed Herodotus: he wrote that Egyptian women went to market while the men stayed home and wove. Look for a woman's name inside a cartouche: that signals real power.

summary: A broken slab from a French fort and an obsessive young linguist from Figeac unlocked 3,000 years of Egyptian writing in 1822.
look: The real stone is in the British Museum in London; here you will meet copies, and its three scripts all over Egypt. Its top band is hieroglyphs, the middle demotic, the everyday cursive script, the bottom Greek. Every cartouche you spell out on this trip uses the method Champollion worked out from it.
story:
Napoleon's invasion of 1798 brought scholars as well as soldiers; their survey became the Description de l'Egypte. In July 1799 the officer Pierre-Francois Bouchard found the stone reused in Fort Julien near Rashid. It is granodiorite from the Aswan region, about 112 centimetres high and 760 kilograms, a fragment of a larger stela. Its decree, passed by priests at Memphis on 27 March 196 BC, honours Ptolemy V in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Under the Capitulation of Alexandria the British took it in 1801; it has been in the British Museum since 1802, and Egyptian scholars have called for its return.

The Greek was translated by 1803. Johan David Akerblad and Thomas Young made progress with demotic, and Young showed that cartouches held royal names spelled phonetically. Champollion, born in Figeac in 1790, had studied Coptic since his teens, convinced it was the last form of Egyptian. In September 1822, after matching the signs in the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, he read native names such as Ramesses and Thutmose and realised that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs and meaning signs. Legend says he burst into his brother's office, cried 'Je tiens l'affaire!', I've got it, and fainted. His Precis of 1824 set out the system; some accused him of not crediting Young.

In 1828 and 1829 he finally toured Egypt and Nubia, reading inscriptions at Karnak, the Valley of the Kings and Abu Simbel. Worn out by the journey, he died in Paris in 1832, aged 41. His Egyptian grammar was published after his death.
details: Rosetta Stone: about 112 centimetres high and 760 kilograms; only the last 14 lines of its hieroglyphic text survive.
Demotic, the middle script, looks like rows of hooks and dashes: everyday handwriting descended from hieroglyphs.
Coptic, still used in Egyptian church services, is Egyptian written in Greek letters plus a few extra signs.
Philae (Aswan): an obelisk taken from there to England gave scholars Cleopatra's cartouche to set beside Ptolemy's.
In a Ptolemy cartouche the recumbent lion stands for L: one of Champollion's first footholds.
fun_fact: For almost two centuries the stone was thought to be black basalt; a 1999 cleaning removed old chalk and wax and revealed grey granodiorite with a pink vein.
narration: Every time you read a royal name on this trip, thank two things: a broken stone and a stubborn young man. In July 1799, French soldiers rebuilding a fort at Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, found a dark slab built into a wall. It carried one decree in 3 scripts: hieroglyphs at the top, demotic, the everyday Egyptian handwriting, in the middle, and Greek at the bottom. Priests had issued it in 196 BC to honour the young king Ptolemy the Fifth. Since scholars could read Greek, here was a crib. The British took the stone in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum ever since. The race to read it ran for 20 years. The English polymath Thomas Young saw that the ovals held royal names. But Jean-Francois Champollion, from Figeac, had a secret weapon: Coptic, the last stage of Egyptian, which he spoke to himself and claimed to dream in. Using the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, he matched signs to sounds. Then, in September 1822, he read the names Ramesses and Thutmose and saw that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs with picture signs. Family legend says he ran to his brother shouting I've got it, and fainted. In 1828 and 1829 he finally travelled up the Nile, reading walls no one had read for some 1,400 years. He died at 41. Look at any Ptolemy cartouche: the lion is an L, and that is where it all began.
